subject: Culture
title: Stolen Recipes
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Stolen Recipes.

hook.text: The British took tea from China and grew it in India. They didn't ask permission.

buildup.text: Colonial powers relocated crops and recipes to their own territories. Rubber, coffee, tea—all transplanted.

discovery.text: Robert Fortune smuggled tea plants from China to India in 1848. An act of agricultural espionage.

twist.text: India now produces more tea than China. The stolen plant became the colony's most famous export.

climax.text: Food doesn't just cross borders. It gets taken, replanted, and rebranded by the powerful.

punchline.text: Your favorite tea has a heist story behind it.

quiz.question: Who smuggled tea plants from China to India in 1848?

details.summary: Recipe theft and food appropriation occur when dominant cultures commercialize dishes from marginalized communities without credit or compensation. From the uncredited African American origins of Southern cuisine to corporate patenting of traditional indigenous recipes, food theft is a form of.
details.whyItMatters: Food appropriation strips communities of cultural ownership and economic benefit. Recognizing stolen recipes is essential for food justice and giving credit where it is due.
takeaways: Much of American Southern cuisine has uncredited African American origins
Corporations have attempted to patent traditional indigenous recipes
Food appropriation debates center on credit, profit, and power

faq.question: How is Southern cuisine an example of food theft?
faq.answer: Enslaved Africans brought techniques like deep-frying, one-pot cooking, and specific ingredient combinations (okra, rice, black-eyed peas) that became 'Southern cooking.' White plantation owners and later cookbook authors systematically erased these origins.

faq.question: Can a recipe be stolen?
faq.answer: Legally, recipes are difficult to patent or copyright (ingredient lists are not copyrightable). Culturally, the issue is credit and profit. When a chef from a dominant culture profits from a marginalized community's dish without acknowledgment, it parallels other forms of cultural extraction.
